title: "Unique IDs Across Go Service Instances"

# Unique IDs Across Go Service Instances

A mutex makes an increment unique inside one process. It cannot prevent a second process from issuing the same value. Choose IDs according to the property required: uniqueness, compact storage, approximate time order, unpredictability, or coordination-free generation.

| Strategy | Benefit | Cost or limit |
|----------|---------|---------------|
| Database sequence | Simple centralized allocation | Database dependency; gaps are normal |
| Random 128-bit ID | Independent writers | Probabilistic uniqueness; no time ordering |
| Time/node/sequence integer | Compact, roughly time ordered | Worker allocation and clock rollback policy |

An identifier is not an access-control secret. An unguessable-looking value still requires authorization, and a timestamp-bearing ID can reveal timing.

## Random IDs: a small Go baseline

Save as `main.go` and run `go run main.go`:

```go
package main

import (
	"crypto/rand"
	"encoding/hex"
	"fmt"
)

func NewID() string {
	var b [16]byte
	rand.Read(b[:])
	return hex.EncodeToString(b[:])
}

func main() {
	a, b := NewID(), NewID()
	fmt.Println("length:", len(a))
	fmt.Println("distinct:", a != b)
}
```

Expected output is length `32` and, with overwhelming probability, `distinct: true`. These are opaque random IDs, not a UUID wire format. The [crypto/rand documentation](https://pkg.go.dev/crypto/rand) describes the randomness source. Put a uniqueness constraint on stored IDs and retry a conflicting insert without overwriting data.

For `n` independent IDs in a space of size `N`, the small-probability birthday approximation is `n(n−1)/(2N)`. At one billion 128-bit IDs it is about `1.5 × 10^-21`. A test that samples a million IDs cannot prove uniqueness.

## Time/node/sequence design exercise

Reserve one sign bit and allocate 41 timestamp bits (milliseconds since a custom epoch), 10 worker bits, and 12 sequence bits:

```text
ID = elapsedMilliseconds << 22 | workerID << 12 | sequence
```

This gives 1,024 worker slots and 4,096 values per millisecond per worker, with about 69.7 years of timestamp range. That is a bit budget, not a throughput measurement. Validate every range before shifting.

In Go, keep `lastMillisecond` and `sequence` behind a mutex. Inject a clock interface for deterministic tests. On the same millisecond increment the sequence; on overflow wait with context cancellation or return a retryable exhaustion error. If wall time moves backward, stop issuing values until a stated recovery condition holds. Never silently reuse an old timestamp and sequence.

Unique worker IDs require a coordination protocol. A lease expiry alone cannot stop a partitioned old process from generating IDs; use an allocator design that prevents overlapping use, a fenced downstream write protocol, or choose random IDs instead. A restarted worker must also avoid reissuing values from its previous lifetime.

## Build and verify

Expose `Next(ctx context.Context) (uint64, error)` for the coordinated generator, and return IDs as JSON strings when consumers may lose integer precision. Record the epoch and layout as part of the storage contract.

Use a fake clock to test identical milliseconds, sequence exhaustion, backward movement, timestamp overflow, restart, and conflicting worker ownership. Verify a million concurrent calls with `go test -race`; then deliberately configure two independent generators with one worker ID to demonstrate the coordination failure. Use the [URL shortener extension](../99-projects/99b-url-shortener-api.qmd#system-design-extension-durable-short-links) to compare allocation strategies under a database uniqueness constraint.
